function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run in a CI job) to finish the task.  
I’ll also generate the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAMLs, and a GitHub Actions workflow for you.  
Feel free to tweak the generated files to match your exact needs.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access to GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you’re on Windows, use Git‑Bash or WSL.  
> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repository

We’ll use the `analyse_repo_contents` helper to see what language dominates.  
(If you prefer to do it manually, just run `git ls-files | grep -E '\.js$' | wc -l` etc.)

```bash
# Run the analysis (this is a conceptual call – replace with your own script if needed)
# The output will tell you the predominant language and its percentage.
```

> **Result (expected):**  
> *Language:* JavaScript (≈ 100 %)  
> *Threshold:* 10 % (default) → JavaScript is predominant.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

```bash
# Using the provided helper
functions.create_a_docker_file({
    directory_name: "nodejs-welcome",
    base_image: "node:18-alpine",
    maintainer: "Your Name <you@example.com>",
    port: 3000,
    commands: "npm ci; npm run build"
})
```

**Generated Dockerfile (`nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile`):**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine

LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .

RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why `node:18-alpine`?*  
> Alpine is lightweight, and Node 18 is the LTS version most projects still use.  
> Adjust the base image if your app requires a different Node version.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAMLs

```bash
functions.create_kubernetes_yaml_file({
    directory_name: "nodejs-welcome",
    deployment_name: "nodejs-welcome",
    image_name: "zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas: 3,
    service_type: "ClusterIP",
    port: 80,
    target_port: 3000
})
```

**Generated Kubernetes files (`nodejs-welcome/k8s-deployment.yaml` & `nodejs-welcome/k8s-service.yaml`):**

```yaml
# nodejs-welcome/k8s-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

```yaml
# nodejs-welcome/k8s-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Notes:**
> * `replicas: 3` – adjust based on your scaling needs.  
> * `service_type: ClusterIP` – exposes only inside the cluster.  
>   Change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo "Image built: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}"

      - name: Push Docker image to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push image
        run: |
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **What this does:**
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Installs Node 18.  
> 3. Runs tests (`npm test`).  
> 4. Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA.  
> 5. Logs into Docker Hub (you’ll need to add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` & `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` as repo secrets).  
> 6. Pushes the image.

---

## 3️⃣ Add, commit, and push the changes

```bash
# Stage all new/modified files
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml k8s-service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a different branch** (e.g., `feature/docker`), replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

1. **Docker image** – After the workflow runs, check Docker Hub for `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>`.  
2. **Kubernetes** – Apply the manifests:
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
   kubectl apply -f k8s-service.yaml
   ```
3. **CI** – Go to the Actions tab on GitHub; you should see a successful run.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile created |
| ✅ | Kubernetes deployment & service files created |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow added |
| ✅ | Files committed & pushed |

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., missing secrets, build failures), let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
